stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Sotelo's hypothesis?
stimulus: Obsidian blades are abundant at Ravna Kosa, a hilltop settlement occupied around 3000 BCE, yet the nearest obsidian source is a volcanic field some 300 kilometers away. Producing a blade from a raw obsidian core generates hundreds of small flakes and chips, debris that typically accumulates wherever the knapping takes place. Archaeologist Mira Sotelo hypothesizes that the settlement's residents did not make the blades themselves but instead received them as finished tools.
choices: Chemical analysis shows that the blades' obsidian matches the composition of rock from the volcanic field 300 kilometers away.
Excavations across the settlement have recovered very few of the small obsidian flakes and chips produced during blade making.
Microscopic wear on the blades' edges indicates that most of them were used to cut plant fibers rather than meat.
Several large, partially worked obsidian cores have been recovered from the floors of houses at the settlement.
explanation: The claim's key term is 'finished tools': the blades were not made at Ravna Kosa. The passage tells you that making blades leaves heaps of flakes wherever the work happens. If almost no such debris turns up at the site, the knapping probably happened somewhere else, so the blades arrived already made. That makes the claim more likely.

A.why: You picked a true-sounding, on-topic fact that doesn't touch the claim. The passage already says the obsidian came from far away. What's in question is whether it arrived as finished blades or as raw cores, and a chemical match can't tell those apart.

C.why: You picked a detail about how the blades were used. The claim is about where they were made, and edge wear says nothing about that.

D.why: Partly worked cores inside houses would mean residents were making blades themselves, which weakens Sotelo's hypothesis rather than supporting it.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's hypothesis?
stimulus: Many coral larvae settle preferentially on crustose coralline algae, a pink alga that coats reef rock. The algae offer both a distinctive rough surface and chemical compounds released by living cells. To separate these factors, a team placed larvae in two tanks. One held tiles coated with live algae; the other held tiles bearing algae that had been killed and bleached, which kept the same rough surface but released no compounds. The team hypothesized that chemical cues, not surface texture, drive the larvae's preference.
choices: Larvae settled at much higher rates on tiles coated with live algae than on smooth tiles that had no algae at all.
Larvae that settled on tiles coated with live algae grew faster during their first month than larvae on other surfaces.
Larvae settled at similar rates on tiles coated with live algae and on tiles bearing algae that had been killed and bleached.
Larvae settled at much higher rates on tiles coated with live algae than on tiles bearing algae that had been killed and bleached.
explanation: The two tanks match on texture and differ only in chemical cues. If the hypothesis is right, larvae should strongly prefer the live-algae tiles over the dead-algae tiles, even though both surfaces are equally rough. That is exactly what this choice reports.

A.why: You picked a result that supports a broader idea: larvae prefer algae. Smooth bare tiles differ from live-algae tiles in both texture and chemistry, so this result can't show which factor matters, and that is the whole claim.

B.why: You picked a fact about growth after settling. The hypothesis is about what makes larvae choose where to settle.

C.why: If larvae settled equally on both tiles, removing the chemical cues changed nothing. That points to texture and weakens the hypothesis.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Anand's claim?
stimulus: Some self-healing plastics contain tiny capsules of liquid healing agent scattered among particles of a catalyst. When a crack forms, it ruptures nearby capsules; the released liquid flows into the crack, where contact with the catalyst makes it harden and bond the crack shut. Samples tested at -20°C recover far less of their original strength than samples tested at room temperature. Materials scientist Priya Anand argues that the cold does not prevent the capsules from breaking but instead slows the hardening reaction.
choices: In cracked cold samples, the capsules along the crack were broken and empty, but the liquid inside the crack had not hardened.
Cracked cold samples recovered less than a third of their original strength, while room-temperature samples recovered nearly all of it.
In cracked cold samples, most of the capsules along the crack were still intact and full of liquid healing agent.
At room temperature, samples containing more capsules recovered more strength than samples containing fewer capsules.
explanation: Anand's claim has two parts: the capsules still break in the cold, and the failure happens later, at the hardening step. Empty capsules show the liquid was released. Unhardened liquid in the crack shows the reaction is where the process stalled. Both parts are confirmed.

B.why: You picked a choice that just repeats, with numbers, the weaker recovery the passage already describes. Anand is explaining why that happens, and this choice doesn't say which step failed.

C.why: Intact capsules would mean the cold stopped them from breaking. That is the very explanation Anand rejects.

D.why: You picked a fact about how many capsules there are, and only at room temperature. It says nothing about what the cold does to the process.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Irigoyen's claim?
stimulus: In many cities, songbirds sing at a higher pitch than members of the same species in the countryside, a shift that may help their songs carry over low-frequency traffic noise. The difference could arise because urban populations have gradually developed fixed, higher-pitched songs over many generations. Ornithologist Tomás Irigoyen, however, contends that individual birds adjust their pitch flexibly, raising it only when the surrounding noise is loud.
choices: Across twelve cities, songbirds' average pitch was higher in cities with heavy traffic than in cities with light traffic.
Songbirds living in cities were found to begin singing earlier each morning than songbirds living in the countryside.
The same individual birds sang at a higher pitch during weekday rush hours than during quiet weekend mornings.
Chicks of urban birds raised in quiet aviaries developed the same high-pitched songs as their parents.
explanation: The key terms are 'individual' and 'flexibly'. Irigoyen says one bird changes its pitch as the noise changes. If the same birds sing higher when traffic is loud and lower when it's quiet, that is flexible adjustment within each bird.

A.why: You picked a result that links noise and pitch, which is broader than the claim. A comparison between cities fits fixed, inherited songs just as well as flexible ones, so it can't settle the question Irigoyen is answering.

B.why: You picked a fact about when birds sing. The claim is about pitch and noise.

D.why: Chicks that develop high songs even without noise suggest the pitch is fixed and inherited. That is the alternative Irigoyen argues against.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Marsh's conclusion?
stimulus: Anders Holt's 1672 chart of the northern Baltic coast was prized by navigators for its detailed depiction of harbors and inlets, though its interior regions are sketchy and often misplaced. Holt left no account of how he gathered his information. After studying the chart, historian Lena Marsh concluded that Holt drew the coastline not from surveys of his own but by compiling the written logs kept by ship pilots.
choices: Holt's chart depicts the region's harbors and inlets far more accurately than any earlier chart of the region does.
Harbor names on Holt's chart repeat unusual misspellings found in surviving pilots' logs from the same decade.
Holt's chart was copied by several later mapmakers, some of whom still relied on it as late as the 1720s.
Holt's account books record wages he paid to a survey crew during the years he worked on the chart.
explanation: Marsh's conclusion names a specific source: pilots' written logs. If the chart repeats the logs' own odd spellings, Holt was very likely copying from those documents. That points straight at the source she identifies.

A.why: You picked an accurate, on-topic fact about how good the chart is. Accurate coastlines could come from Holt's own surveys or from pilots' logs, so this doesn't show where his information came from.

C.why: You picked a fact about the chart's later influence. The claim is about how Holt gathered his information in the first place.

D.why: Paying a survey crew suggests Holt did his own surveying, which is what Marsh concluded he did not do.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okafor's argument?
stimulus: Over the past decade, a new pronunciation of the vowel in words such as "fell" has spread among teenagers in the city of Harlow Bay, having first appeared in a single eastern neighborhood. Some researchers attribute the spread to popular online videos featuring speakers from that neighborhood. Linguist Dana Okafor, however, argues that the pronunciation has spread chiefly through teenagers' face-to-face friendships rather than through media exposure.
choices: Teenagers with close friends from the eastern neighborhood adopted the pronunciation early, whether or not they watched the videos.
Teenagers throughout the city use the new pronunciation far more often than their parents and grandparents do.
Teenagers who watched the videos adopted the pronunciation early, even if they had no friends from the eastern neighborhood.
A similar vowel change spread through a neighboring city about fifty years before it appeared in Harlow Bay.
explanation: Okafor's claim sets friendships against media. This finding separates the two: having friends from the neighborhood predicts early adoption, and watching the videos doesn't. That is the pattern her argument predicts.

B.why: You picked a choice that confirms teenagers are driving the change, which the passage already assumes. It says nothing about whether friendships or media spread it.

C.why: If watching the videos is enough without any friendships, that supports the media explanation Okafor rejects.

D.why: You picked a historical parallel in another city. It doesn't tell you how the pronunciation is spreading in Harlow Bay.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' hypothesis?
stimulus: Mice raised in sterile conditions, without gut bacteria, respond weakly to certain vaccines, suggesting that gut microbes help the immune system develop. To test when such exposure matters, researchers gave one group of these germ-free mice gut bacteria shortly after birth and gave an otherwise identical group the same bacteria as adults, then vaccinated both groups. The researchers hypothesized that microbial exposure strengthens vaccine responses only if it occurs early in life.
choices: Germ-free mice that never received gut bacteria responded to the vaccine more weakly than mice raised in ordinary conditions.
Mice given bacteria shortly after birth gained weight faster in their first month than mice that stayed germ-free.
Mice given bacteria shortly after birth and mice given bacteria as adults responded to the vaccine equally strongly.
Mice given bacteria shortly after birth responded strongly to the vaccine, but mice given bacteria as adults responded weakly.
explanation: The deciding words are 'only if' and 'early in life'. The hypothesis predicts a gap between the groups: exposure right after birth helps, and exposure in adulthood doesn't. A strong response in the newborn group and a weak one in the adult group is that gap.

A.why: You picked a choice that supports the broader idea that microbes matter, which the passage already states. It says nothing about timing, and timing is the entire hypothesis.

B.why: You picked a fact about weight gain. The hypothesis is about vaccine responses.

C.why: Equal responses would mean the timing of exposure makes no difference, which weakens the 'only if early' hypothesis.

stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Petrov's claim?
stimulus: Summer thunderstorms occur more often downwind of some large cities than upwind of them. One explanation holds that pavement and buildings heat the air above the city, which rises and forms storm clouds. Another holds that airborne particles from traffic and industry give water vapor surfaces on which to condense, seeding clouds. Meteorologist Ivan Petrov maintains that the city's heat, not its particle pollution, is the main trigger of the extra storms.
choices: Most of the airborne particles over the city come from vehicle traffic rather than from factories and power plants.
Summer thunderstorms occur roughly 25 percent more often in areas downwind of the city than in areas upwind of it.
On days when airborne particle levels were unusually low, the downwind increase in storms was as large as on typical days.
On unusually cool summer days, the downwind increase in storms was as large as on the hottest days of the season.
explanation: Petrov compares two causes and ranks heat above particles. If storms stay just as frequent when particles are scarce, particles can't be the main trigger. That leaves heat as the better explanation.

A.why: You picked a fact about where the particles come from. Both traffic and industry fall under the particle explanation, so this doesn't separate it from the heat explanation.

B.why: You picked a choice that just puts a number on the pattern both explanations are trying to account for. It doesn't favor heat over particles.

D.why: If the extra storms continue even when the city is cool, heat is not the trigger. That weakens Petrov's claim.
